entries.title: Affixes, slots, and templates
entries.description: An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A prefix comes before it, a suffix after it, and an infix inside it. As illustrative English examples, un-happy shows a prefix and kind-ness a suffix. The Turkish form evler (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to ev (“house”).
entries.helpPage:
# Affixes, slots, and templates

An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A **prefix** comes before it, a **suffix** after it, and an **infix** inside it. As illustrative English examples, *un-happy* shows a prefix and *kind-ness* a suffix. The Turkish form *evler* (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to *ev* (“house”).

Languages often restrict which affixes can combine and in what order. A **slot** is a position in that sequence. For example, an illustrative verb pattern might allow a person marker before a tense marker. Putting the same affixes in the reverse order could produce a form the language does not use.

In FieldWorks, affix templates organize slots for a part of speech. A noun template can describe noun patterns, while a verb template can describe verb patterns. Some slots are obligatory: a valid word using that template must fill them. Others are optional and may be skipped. These settings help the parser avoid treating every affix as freely combinable with every word.

When a trace reaches the right stem but stops before the expected ending, check the relevant template. Is the affix in the right slot? Is the order right? Is the slot required or optional as intended? Does the template apply to this part of speech? Keep one known word that should use the pattern and one similar word that should not; both help you check whether the template says what you mean.

The examples here are illustrative and simplified. Real languages can have several templates, and a slot can allow more than one affix.

entries.title: Allomorphs and environments
entries.description: One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are allomorphs. The conditions that choose between them are their environments: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.
entries.helpPage:
# Allomorphs and environments

One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are **allomorphs**. The conditions that choose between them are their **environments**: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.

Turkish vowel harmony is a useful real-language example. The plural suffix has the forms *-lar* and *-ler*. In the standard pattern, *-lar* follows a stem with a back last vowel, as in *okullar* (“schools”), and *-ler* follows a stem with a front last vowel, as in *evler* (“houses”). The forms belong to the same plural pattern; the stem’s vowel helps select which one fits.

A **natural class** groups sounds by a shared property, such as “front vowels” or “voiceless consonants.” Instead of writing a separate environment for every vowel, a grammar can use a natural class when the same condition applies to that group. This can make a rule clearer and easier to check.

When the parser builds the stem but cannot use the expected affix form, compare the allomorphs and their environments. Does the needed form exist? Does its environment mention the right sounds or features? Is the environment too narrow, so it misses a valid word, or too broad, so it allows the form where it does not belong?

The Turkish forms illustrate a common pattern; they are not a full account of Turkish. Real patterns may depend on additional features and exceptions.

entries.title: Teach a dumb computer your language
entries.description: You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.
entries.helpPage:
# Teach a dumb computer your language

You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.

The work is a loop:

1. **Measure.** Save your FieldWorks work, then choose **Refresh** or run an [Assessment](term:assessment) to measure words you care about. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) tells you how much of the chosen material parsed.
2. **Understand.** Try a difficult word in **Try a Word**. Read the parser’s furthest attempt, then follow its steps to see what it built and where it stopped. Use **Timing** when words take a long time.
3. **Fix.** Use your language knowledge to check the likely cause. Make any grammar or lexicon change in FieldWorks, save it, and measure again.

Motif's synthetic samples are generated to demonstrate its tools and give us small, safe places to practise. They are synthetic-turkic (Turkish-style), synthetic-bantu (Swahili-style), and synthetic-philippine (Tagalog-style), each modelled loosely on the named language. Their data are invented: they are not real language data and must not be used as descriptions of Turkish, Swahili, Tagalog, or any language.

You do not need to become a parser engineer to take part. You can tell an AI consultant what a word should mean and how it is built. Ask it to connect that analysis to the trace, suggest one small change, and name other words that should test the idea. Then check the suggestion against your language knowledge and Motif’s evidence. The AI can help with the machinery; it cannot decide what is right in your language.

entries.title: Modelling a grammar the parser can use
entries.description: FieldWorks will save a grammar the parser cannot fully use, and it will not always tell you. An environment with a typing mistake can quietly stop restricting its allomorph, and a slot with no working affix can drop out of its template. This page lists the habits that keep what you model in FieldWorks the same as what the parser actually runs.
entries.helpPage:
# Modelling a grammar the parser can use

FieldWorks will save a grammar the parser cannot fully use, and it will not always tell you. An environment with a typing mistake can quietly stop restricting its allomorph, and a slot with no working affix can drop out of its template. This page lists the habits that keep what you model in FieldWorks the same as what the parser actually runs.

## Start from the language, then check it arrived

Write down what each part of your grammar means before you enter it: "the plural is *-ler* after front vowels and *-lar* after back vowels." After you save, don't take a clean save as proof. Choose **Check the grammar** on **Warnings**, and then measure words that should use each part. Something you entered that no word needs is still unproven.

## Sounds and spellings

The parser only knows the sounds in your first phoneme set, spelled the way their codes say. A sound with no code, or two sounds spelled the same way, is left out. So is any natural class that contains that sound, as a whole. When a word fails near an unusual letter, check its phoneme and code first.

## Environments

An environment such as `/ [V] _` says where an allomorph may occur. Check each one after you type it: a mistake in an affix's environment can leave that allomorph allowed everywhere, so the word still parses and nothing looks wrong. For an infix, the position environment uses `#` for the start of the stem, not the edge of the word: `/# [C] _` puts the infix after the first consonant.

## Allomorph order

When several allomorphs of one morpheme could fit, the first eligible one wins and blocks the rest. Put the most specific allomorph first and the general one last.

## Slots and templates

Every inflectional affix needs a slot in a template, and every slot needs at least one affix the parser can load. A slot with no usable affix disappears, and a template whose slots all disappear is dropped. **Warnings** reports inflectional affixes that have no slot.

## Features and classes

Features, their values, and inflection classes link by reference, not by name: two things with the same name are not connected. A noun-class system can use both an inflection class and a feature value for each class, as the synthetic Bantu-style sample does, but test agreement on real words before you rely on it.

## What the parser does not run yet

The PanGloss parser that Motif uses (version 0.5) does not yet run some things FieldWorks lets you model:

- **Reduplication** written as a copy pattern such as `[C^1][V^1]-` is not loaded. Infixes such as *-um-* do work.
- **Metathesis rules** are skipped.
- **Custom strata** in the parser settings are read but not applied.

Model them if your analysis needs them, and expect words that depend on them not to parse yet.

## When a grammar is slow

Parse time comes from the paths the parser has to try. Optional slots, broad environments and duplicated affixes can each add paths, but no single kind of choice is always costly. In the synthetic Bantu-style sample, 160 empty allomorphs added no measurable work, while one duplicated real affix multiplied it. Use [Timing](cmd:timing) after an [Assessment](term:assessment) to see where the work actually went. The Learn page **Why a grammar is slow** shows how to read it.

## Change one thing at a time

After each change: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, and check the words you expected to change, plus a few that shouldn't. One change per measurement tells you what each change did.

entries.title: Phonological rules
entries.description: When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonological rules

When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.

English plural endings give an illustrative example of a familiar sound pattern. The ending is usually pronounced with a voiceless [s] after a voiceless sound, as in *cats*, and with [z] after a voiced sound, as in *dogs*. After sibilant sounds, as in *buses*, an extra vowel is heard. These examples show how nearby sounds can affect the way an ending is pronounced; spelling alone does not show every sound detail.

A rule says what changes and in what environment. In plain words, one part of this pattern could be described as “make the ending voiced after a voiced sound.” A well-chosen rule covers the words that share that environment. A rule that is too broad can also change words you meant to leave alone, so check examples from both sides of the pattern.

Rule order matters when one rule changes something that another rule looks for. If Rule 1 creates the sound that Rule 2 needs to see, Rule 1 must apply first. If Rule 2 applies first, it cannot act on a sound that does not exist yet. When a trace shows an unexpected output, check both the rule’s environment and whether earlier rules have already changed the relevant sound.

entries.title: Reading why a word fails
entries.description: Try a Word traces a word through the grammar in the current Baseline. The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project’s Texts or lexicon. Enter it in Type any word..., choose Try it, and read the result. You can cancel a running trace.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading why a word fails

**Try a Word** traces a word through the grammar in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project’s Texts or lexicon. Enter it in **Type any word...**, choose **Try it**, and read the result. You can cancel a running trace.

Start with the answer and search status:

- **Parsed** means the parser found an analysis.
- **No parse** with **Search complete** means it finished and found no analysis.
- **Search incomplete** gives the stop reason when the parser did not finish. A limit is not evidence that no analysis exists.
- **Nothing to parse** means the word has a character the grammar’s character table does not define.

For a failed word, look at **THE PARSER'S FURTHEST TRY** and the rule steps. The attempt shows the pieces it built and the rule that stopped it, when recorded. If it never gets a stem, begin with the lexicon. If it builds a stem but stops at an affix, check the slot order and the affix’s allomorph or environment. If a rule changes an unexpected sound, inspect the phonological rules and their order.

The trace is a record of the parser’s search, not a verdict about the word. A rule can stop one attempt while another attempt succeeds. A completed **No parse** can have several plausible causes, so compare the trace with the form and analysis you know are right. If the search was incomplete, adjust the relevant limit and try again before changing the grammar.

entries.title: Stems and the lexicon
entries.description: The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.
entries.helpPage:
# Stems and the lexicon

The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.

As an illustrative English example, *walk* is the stem, *to move on foot* is a possible gloss, and *verb* is its part of speech. The form *walked* can be built from that stem and a past-tense ending. A gloss is a short guide for people, not a complete definition or a promise that two languages divide meaning in the same way.

One of the most common causes of failure is a missing stem. If a grammar expects to start with *walk* but that stem is absent or entered under a different form, adding the ending rule will not give the parser a starting point. In a simplified, illustrative Turkish example, the stem *ev* (“house”) is needed before the grammar can analyse *evler* (“houses”) with the plural suffix.

When a word fails, compare the form you typed with the lexicon entry you expect. Check spelling and the relevant writing system, then check that the entry has the stem and part of speech your analysis requires. If the stem is there, move on to the affixes and rules that should build the rest of the word.

The examples here are illustrative; real entries and analyses depend on the language and the choices made in its FieldWorks project.

entries.title: What the parser knows
entries.description: A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current Baseline. It does not know what you meant, guess a missing entry from the conversation, or silently repair a rule.
entries.helpPage:
# What the parser knows

A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). It does not know what you meant, guess a missing entry from the conversation, or silently repair a rule.

A **parse** is an analysis the grammar can build for a word. As an illustrative English example, *cats* can be analysed as the stem *cat* plus the plural ending *-s*. The parser must find a matching stem and a permitted way to combine it with the ending. A word can have more than one possible analysis, and a completed search may find none.

That makes “it doesn’t parse” useful information. It says that, for this word and this saved grammar, the parser did not build an analysis. The result can narrow your next question: Is the stem present? Is the ending allowed after this kind of stem? Does its form fit the sound environment? Is a sound rule changing the form?

First check whether the search completed. A completed search with **No parse** tells you the grammar did not produce a reading. **Search incomplete** means the parser stopped before finishing; a time or step limit can cause that, so it cannot show that the grammar has no possible analysis. A word with a character missing from the grammar’s character table is a different case again.

The parser reports what its grammar allowed. You decide whether that grammar matches the language.

entries.title: Why a grammar is slow
entries.description: A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Why a grammar is slow

A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.

An optional slot lets the parser consider a form both with and without that slot. Broad environments let a rule apply in many places, creating more possible continuations. An empty affix adds no visible letters, so the parser can add it without consuming part of the word, though PanGloss often handles these cheaply: in the synthetic Bantu-style sample, 160 empty allomorphs added no measurable work. A duplicated real affix is different; there, copying one object marker into a second slot multiplied the work.

Use [Timing](cmd:timing) after an [Assessment](term:assessment) to locate recorded parse time. **Timing** groups time first by kind of rule, then by rule, and then shows slow words. Start with **Slowest** or **All**, select a costly rule, and look at the words that use it. A single unusually slow word may point to its stem or environment; a costly rule affecting many words may be a broader pattern to review.

Check that each optional slot is truly optional, each environment names the sounds it should, and each affix appears only once. Change one thing at a time and measure again. If the search stopped at a step limit, more time will not fix that outcome; choose a larger step limit for the rerun. A timing result shows where work was spent, while your language knowledge helps decide whether the grammar can be made more specific.

entries.title: Working with an AI consultant
entries.description: You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: AI Handoff writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, an Assessment with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with an AI consultant

You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: **AI Handoff** writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, an [Assessment](term:assessment) with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.

Ask a focused question. For example: “This word should be stem plus plural. The trace stops at this affix. Which slot or environment would you check first? What evidence supports that, and what other words would distinguish your suggestion from an alternative?” Ask for one small proposed change and examples that should still fail. You can ask the AI to explain parser terminology, but check every claim about your language against what speakers say and use.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis, not an instruction. Check that it accounts for the failing word without breaking a known-good word. If you decide to change the grammar or lexicon, make the edit in FieldWorks, save, then choose **Refresh** and inspect the new evidence in Motif.

**Review changes** has a narrower role: it reviews pending analysis choices made in Motif. If the AI suggests choosing or changing an analysis for a word, make that choice through **Texts**, then open **Review changes**. Inspect the word and action, choose **Check these changes** to measure their effect, and apply only if the changes still fit and the evidence is current. Review changes does not import an AI answer or apply grammar edits; your judgement remains in charge.

entries.title: Opening a project
entries.description: Open the project menu and choose Select new… to browse for a FieldWorks .fwdata file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose Open recent and select it. The window opens on Overview and reads the project’s stored Baseline, Selection, and results; opening it does not automatically take a new measurement.
entries.helpPage:
# Opening a project

Open the project menu and choose **Select new…** to browse for a FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose **Open recent** and select it. The window opens on **Overview** and reads the project’s stored Baseline, Selection, and results; opening it does not automatically take a new measurement.

If this project has no Baseline yet, press **Refresh**. Motif reads the saved `.fwdata` file to capture the Baseline. Save your latest edits in FieldWorks first if you want them included: unsaved edits in FieldWorks are not part of the file Motif reads. You do not have to close FieldWorks just to open a project, though a capture may be refused while another program holds the project.

For a project without a saved Default Selection, setup opens once a Baseline is available, unless setup was skipped. On a new project, the first **Refresh** captures the Baseline and opens setup. Before that first Baseline, **Configure…** is disabled and its detail reads **Refresh first to choose Texts**. In setup, choose texts or add words, set the parsing limits, and start the first run. You can choose **Skip for now** and use **Configure…** later to reopen setup.

FieldWorks must be closed before you apply changes from Motif. This is separate from opening the project or reading its last saved state.

![A project open on the Overview](shot:open-project-overview/project-opened)

entries.title: Overview
entries.description: Overview is the first page when you open a project. It gathers stored results and project counts so you can see where things stand without starting a new run.
entries.helpPage:
# Overview

**Overview** is the first page when you open a project. It gathers stored results and project counts so you can see where things stand without starting a new run.

The top card shows the project and its [Baseline](term:baseline). Other cards summarize **Text Coverage**, **Accuracy**, **Timing**, and **Warnings**. Text Coverage includes parsed words and occurrences; Accuracy compares parser readings with approved analyses; Timing shows how long parsing took; Warnings are findings from a grammar check. These are separate measures, not one overall score.

If FieldWorks has saved since the Baseline, the Overview marks its numbers as stale. Press **Refresh** when you are ready to capture the saved project and assess the [Default Selection](term:default-selection). Use the card links to open **Texts**, **Timing**, or **Warnings** for more detail. Expand **Project history** to see recorded activity.

![Overview showing stored project results](shot:open-project-overview/headline-numbers)

entries.description: PanGloss parses XAmple and HermitCrab grammars fast. Fully compatible.
entries.helpPage:

entries.title: Pending changes
entries.description: Pending changes are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from Texts and are listed together on Review changes. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”
entries.helpPage:
# Pending changes

Pending changes are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from **Texts** and are listed together on **Review changes**. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”

Use **Remove** to withdraw a choice, or return to **Texts** to make a different choice for the same word and analysis. The list belongs to its project and remains available if you close Motif and open that project again.

Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are collecting or reading these changes. Before applying, use **Check these changes** to measure the touched words, confirm that the evidence is current and complete, and make sure every choice still fits. Then choose **Apply to FieldWorks project** while FieldWorks is closed.

This page describes the window’s “changes not applied yet” wording. The related stored-change concept is linked here as [pending changes](term:proposal).

entries.title: Reading the Overview
entries.description: The Overview brings together the results Motif has already stored. The top of the page shows the project, the number of words in the Selection, text occurrences, and counts of wordforms, rules, and lexemes. Its cards summarize Text Coverage, Accuracy, Timing, and Warnings.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading the Overview

The **Overview** brings together the results Motif has already stored. The top of the page shows the project, the number of words in the Selection, text occurrences, and counts of wordforms, rules, and lexemes. Its cards summarize **Text Coverage**, **Accuracy**, **Timing**, and **Warnings**.

Text Coverage reports how many selected words and text occurrences parsed. Accuracy describes whether approved analyses were kept. Timing summarizes how long parsing took, including a median and slow words. Warnings are findings from a grammar check; they are about the grammar, not a count of errors in the selected texts. These numbers answer different questions, so read the labels and breakdowns rather than comparing the headline values as if they were one score.

If FieldWorks has saved changes since Motif’s [Baseline](term:baseline), the window marks the stored results as stale. Press **Refresh** to capture the saved project again and measure the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection). Refresh is an explicit action; simply reopening the window does not rerun the parser.

Open **Project history** near the bottom of the page to see recorded activity. Choose a card’s link, such as **Texts →**, **Timing →**, or **Warnings →**, to inspect that information on its page.

![Updated Overview after Refresh](shot:refresh-stale-numbers/updated-overview)

entries.title: Refreshing numbers
entries.description: Use Refresh after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif’s results to reflect that saved state. Refresh is an action, not an automatic update: it captures a new Baseline from the saved project, checks the grammar for Warnings, and assesses the current Default Selection, when one is available.
entries.helpPage:
# Refreshing numbers

Use **Refresh** after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif’s results to reflect that saved state. Refresh is an action, not an automatic update: it captures a new [Baseline](term:baseline) from the saved project, checks the grammar for **Warnings**, and assesses the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection), when one is available.

1. Save your work in FieldWorks.
2. In Motif, choose **Refresh** in the top bar and let it finish.
3. Check the freshness line and the updated cards on **Overview**. The new [Assessment](term:assessment) records what was measured.

If this is the first Baseline, first-time setup may open so you can choose texts or add words before the first Assessment. If you cancel the run or the parser refuses it, the Baseline may still be newer than the numbers; read the freshness message before relying on them. Opening Motif again does not perform a Refresh for you.

![Numbers refreshed against a saved project](shot:refresh-stale-numbers/updated-overview)

entries.title: Changing a pending change
entries.description: You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to Texts, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing a pending change

You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to **Texts**, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.

To remove a change without replacing it:

1. Open **Review changes**.
2. Find the word and action you want to withdraw.
3. Choose **Remove** beside it.

The remaining pending changes stay in the list. Use **Keep editing** to return to the page where the first pending change was collected. Changes belong to the project and remain available if you close Motif and open that project again.

![Replacing a pending change with a new choice](shot:replace-a-pending-change/replaced-choice)

entries.title: Review changes
entries.description: Review changes gathers the analysis changes you have collected from other pages. For each word, it shows the chosen action, the relevant analyses, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Reading this page does not apply anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Review changes

**Review changes** gathers the analysis changes you have collected from other pages. For each word, it shows the chosen action, the relevant analyses, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Reading this page does not apply anything.

1. Check each listed word and action. Choose **Remove** beside a change you no longer want.
2. Choose **Check these changes** to measure the words you touched and see **What applying does to the numbers**. If the check is still running, you can choose **Cancel**.
3. Apply only when the changes still fit, the numbers are current, the evidence is complete, FieldWorks is not holding the project open, and no approved analysis would be lost.
4. Choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. After a successful Apply, the page shows a receipt. There is no extra confirmation step.

If a change says **No longer fits**, Apply stays blocked. Remove that change or refresh the project and check it again. A change that no longer fits cannot be forced. See **When a change no longer fits** for steps to recheck it.

![Review changes and measure their effect](shot:review-changes/measure-changes)

entries.title: Switching projects
entries.description: Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.
entries.helpPage:
# Switching projects

Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.

1. Choose **Select new…** to browse for a `.fwdata` file, or choose **Open recent** and select a project Motif already knows.
2. Wait for the project’s Baseline, Selection, and stored results to load.
3. Check the project name on **Overview** before taking an action.

Each project has its own Motif workflow information. Switching away does not move its pending changes into another project; when you open it again, its changes are shown with that project. If an Assessment or AI Handoff is running, switching projects cancels that work before Motif loads the new project.

Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to reopen the project’s saved Selection and parsing limits. Use **Refresh** when you want a new Baseline and measurement; opening the project alone only reads stored results.

![The Overview after reopening a project](shot:switch-projects/project-reopened)

entries.title: Text Coverage
entries.description: Text Coverage shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their occurrences in the chosen Texts, parsed in a stored Assessment. The Overview reports both selected words and their occurrences, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.
entries.helpPage:
# Text Coverage

[Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their occurrences in the chosen Texts, parsed in a stored Assessment. The Overview reports both selected words and their occurrences, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.

Use the breakdown to see parsed words alongside words with no parse, incomplete searches, or other recorded outcomes. A word that reached a time or step limit did not complete its search, so read that outcome separately from a completed search with no parse.

Text Coverage is about the selected Texts and words. It is not the same as **Accuracy**, which compares parser readings with approved analyses, or grammar coverage over an outside Corpus. Choose **Texts** to inspect words and occurrences; use [Assessment](term:assessment) to understand which run the Overview is showing.

entries.title: Texts
entries.description: Texts is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are Matrix, Analyze texts, Lists, and What changed. In Analyze texts, use Read text to follow words in context or Word list to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use Run assessment to record results for that Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Texts

**Texts** is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are **Matrix**, **Analyze texts**, **Lists**, and **What changed**. In **Analyze texts**, use **Read text** to follow words in context or **Word list** to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use **Run assessment** to record results for that Selection.

The Matrix groups words by their stored project state and parser result. Select a cell to inspect its words, then open a word to see its FieldWorks analyses and parser readings. In the Matrix, available actions include **Approve**, **Disapprove**, **Make Unknown**, **Incorrect spelling**, and **Add as Unknown**. In **Analyze texts**, corresponding actions approve or disapprove a reading, make a reading Unknown, mark a spelling Incorrect, or add parser readings as Unknown. The action applies to the word form everywhere in the project, not only the occurrence currently shown.

Changes you collect remain pending until you review and apply them. The page’s **Review changes** link opens that list; it does not write anything to FieldWorks. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) appears on the Overview after a measurement.

![Text Coverage changing after texts are measured](shot:texts-choose-texts/coverage)

entries.title: Timing
entries.description: Timing shows where recorded parse time went: first by kind of rule, then by rule, then by word. It reads timing stored with an Assessment; opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing yet, run an Assessment first.
entries.helpPage:
# Timing

**Timing** shows where recorded parse time went: first by kind of rule, then by rule, then by word. It reads timing stored with an [Assessment](term:assessment); opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing yet, run an Assessment first.

Under **Look at**, choose **Step limit**, **Slowest**, or **All**. You can also use **Chosen in Texts**, a Matrix cell, a list, or words you enter by hand. The page shows the selected scope’s timing by kind and rule, followed by the slowest words. Select a rule to see the words that cost most under it.

For selected words that need another attempt, use the rerun controls to choose a longer per-word time limit or a larger step limit, then choose **Re-run chosen words**. **Cancel** stops that rerun. More time does not fix a search that reached its step limit; increase the step limit when that is the outcome.

![Slowest words in Timing](shot:timing-slow-words/slowest-words)

entries.title: Try a Word
entries.description: Use Try a Word to trace one word through the grammar in the current Baseline. The word does not need to appear in a chosen text or even exist in the FieldWorks project.
entries.helpPage:
# Try a Word

Use **Try a Word** to trace one word through the grammar in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). The word does not need to appear in a chosen text or even exist in the FieldWorks project.

1. Enter a word in **Type any word...**.
2. Choose **Try it** and wait for the trace. You can choose **Cancel** while it is running.
3. Read whether the word parsed, the project’s expected analyses, and the parser’s furthest attempt. The trace lists rule steps and explains where the search stopped or what each step produced.
4. Use **Open in Texts** to inspect a project word there, or follow a timing link when one is available.

The result distinguishes a completed search with no parse from a search that did not complete; a limit or interrupted search is not evidence that the grammar cannot parse the word. For a detailed trace file, use the diagnostic tools available from this page. A diagnostic can show real word forms and morphology, so inspect it before sharing.

![A word parsed in Try a Word](shot:try-a-word-parses/parsed-word)

entries.helpPage:
# Warnings

**Warnings** shows findings from a check of the whole grammar. They are stored for the [Baseline](term:baseline), and do not depend on which texts or words you selected. Findings do not block an Assessment.

If the grammar has not been checked for this Baseline, choose **Check the grammar**. The parser reads the whole grammar, so a check can take a minute for a large project. **Refresh** also checks the grammar after capturing a Baseline. Later visits use the stored findings until the Baseline changes; opening the page does not start a check by itself.

Use **Where...** to narrow findings by where they apply, or **Problem...** to search by the problem described. Select a finding group to read **What it means** and **What usually helps**. Error-level findings are shown separately from warnings and information. A warning describes what the parser reported; use your linguistic judgment to decide what to investigate or change.

![Filtered grammar findings](shot:warnings-filter/filtered-findings)

# What Motif does

Motif helps you measure how a FieldWorks grammar works, inspect individual words, and collect changes to word analyses before applying them. It reads the saved FieldWorks project; FieldWorks remains the place where the project’s linguistic data lives.

Motif uses PanGloss to parse words. An [Assessment](term:assessment) records what a run measured. The [Overview](term:overview) shows stored results such as Text Coverage, accuracy against approved analyses, timing, and grammar warnings. It does not start a new run just because you open the window.

When you want current numbers, press **Refresh**. Motif captures a [Baseline](term:baseline) from the saved project and measures the project’s [Default Selection](term:default-selection). In **Texts**, you can inspect words and choose analysis changes. **Review changes** lets you check those changes and see whether they still fit before you choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**.

You can also make an **AI Handoff** folder with project context and a question for a chat model. Review the data-sensitivity notice before sharing it: the folder can contain real grammar, lexicon, and text data.

![Motif’s Overview after opening a project](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: When a change no longer fits
entries.description: When a pending change is marked No longer fits, use these steps to check the original choice against the current project.
entries.helpPage:
# When a change no longer fits

When a pending change is marked **No longer fits**, use these steps to check the original choice against the current project.

1. Open **Review changes** and read the reason beside the affected word.
2. If you want to keep trying the change, save the project in FieldWorks, then choose **Refresh** in Motif.
3. On Review changes, choose **Check again against the refreshed project** if it is available. Motif checks whether the original identities still fit.
4. If it still says **No longer fits**, choose **Remove the ones that no longer fit** or remove that change individually. Return to **Texts** and make a new choice against the current project.

Apply remains blocked while any change no longer fits. The window does not offer a way to force a change that no longer fits.

![A change marked No longer fits](shot:no-longer-fits/not-fitting)

entries.title: When something goes wrong
entries.description: If a command or action is refused, first read the message in Motif. It often explains what needs to change, such as saving in FieldWorks, refreshing the Baseline, or removing a change that no longer fits.
entries.helpPage:
# When something goes wrong

If a command or action is refused, first read the message in Motif. It often explains what needs to change, such as saving in FieldWorks, refreshing the Baseline, or removing a change that no longer fits.

For a parser trace, open **Diagnostic tools** from **Try a Word**. You can save or copy diagnostic information for a particular word. It can include real word forms and morphological details, so review it before sharing.

If the app stops after an error, the separate **Motif has stopped** window offers **Copy details**, **Save report**, **Email maintainer**, and **Close**. Include what you were doing, the page, the error message, and steps that reproduce it. Check any saved report or diagnostic for project or linguistic information before sending it to someone else.

![Diagnostic information copied from Motif](shot:copy-diagnostics/copied-diagnostics)
